claims.text: WHO does not endorse a specific hospital laboratory test or clinical prediction algorithm for diagnosing early‑onset neonatal sepsis; it highlights the current lack of simple, universally available tests in many district hospitals.

When laboratory capacity exists, CRP and procalcitonin have shown good discriminatory ability for culture‑confirmed sepsis, but WHO provides no definitive threshold values for clinical decision‑making.

Initial assessment should be based on a comprehensive clinical examination (temperature, respiratory rate, feeding tolerance, activity) and, if feasible, point‑of‑care biomarkers such as CRP or PCT to support the diagnosis.

Continuous monitoring of vital signs (temperature, respiratory rate, SpO₂), feeding adequacy, and neurologic status is essential during the first 72 hours, with reassessment if any parameter deteriorates.

If clinical signs worsen, red‑flag features emerge, or laboratory results become strongly suggestive of sepsis, clinicians should escalate care to a higher‑level facility or specialist team, as WHO notes ongoing work to integrate tests with decision‑support algorithms for timely escalation.

WHO 2024 does not recommend a hospital laboratory or a specific clinical prediction algorithm for diagnosing neonatal sepsis; the guideline emphasizes clinical judgment supplemented by available biomarkers rather than a mandated scoring system.

packet.guideline: WHO serious bacterial infections 2024 (EOS subset), EVALUATION ONLY
packet.evaluation_question: Does WHO 2024 endorse a hospital laboratory or clinical prediction algorithm to diagnose neonatal sepsis? Explain initial assessment without inventing a CBC or CRP threshold. Gestation 40 weeks; age 24 hours; setting hospital.

evidence.text: Two additional systematic reviews examined the diagnostic accuracy of laboratory biomarkers to diagnose culture-confirmed sepsis (88) or clinical or culture-confirmed sepsis (89) in infants aged 0–59 days at the time of presentation to health facilities. Brown et al. (2019) identified 20 studies of 1615 infants reporting upon diagnostic accuracy of CRP in neonates and reported that at median specificity (0.74), sensitivity was 0.62 (95% CI: 0.50 to 0.73) (88). Rees et al. (2023) examined CRP, procalcitonin (PCT), erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) and white cell count (WCC) in 134 studies, and concluded that CRP and PCT demonstrated good discriminatory ability to diagnose sepsis with blood culture as the reference

One further systematic review of seven studies and a total of 505 infants examined the use of CRP in decision-making for stopping antibiotic treatment in newborns diagnosed with sepsis (90). Petel et al. (2018) reported that CRP-based algorithms shortened antibiotic treatment duration by 1.45 days (95% CI: −2.61 to –0.28) in two RCTs, and by 1.15 days (95% CI: −2.06 to –0.24) in two cohort studies, with no differences in mortality or infection relapse in neonates (90).

include laboratory tests due to the lack of availability of simple tests in district hospitals, such as full blood count and C-reactive protein (CRP). However, these tests have become more widely available and POC rapid “bedside” laboratory tests are becoming much more common (10, 75). There has also been much interest in how to integrate laboratory tests with IMCI and other clinical algorithms, and ongoing work to develop more sophisticated predictive algorithms and machine-learning tools to improve sepsis diagnosis, assist clinicians in determining when to stop antibiotics and rationalizing antibiotic therapy (75).
(CRP of ≥ 60 mg/L, AUC: 0.87, 95% CI: 0.76 to 0.91, n=1339 neonates; and PCT of ≥ 0.5 ng/ml, AUC: 0.87, 95% CI: 0.70 to 0.92, n=617 neonates), while ESR and WCC had poor discriminatory ability (89).
